description: Venus, the planet of light and love, turns against the current of the other planets, and burns brightest in the dark night sky.
summary: Venus Echo turns a decade of Sentinel-1 radar into a clear, honest picture of change at the Dead Sea. Radar sees through cloud, capturing what optical sensors cannot, but its raw output is specialist data that few people can read. Our Python pipeline processes 47 OPERA RTC-S1 acquisitions (2016–2026, a single orbit geometry, VV/VH, 30 m) into web-ready layers, change maps and water-area estimates, each with an explicit uncertainty band. These are presented in an open, interactive site covering the whole lake and the Potash City evaporation ponds, with a decade timeline, swipe comparison, charts, and a legend that never relies on color alone. Echo, our in-app guide, explains the science in plain language, quotes only the numbers on screen, and declines to answer what radar cannot know. Built for the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge, Venus Echo uses Sentinel-1 to show these methods at their best, and it is designed for NISAR, the mission this story is really about.
details:
What it does / how it works

  • Fetches Sentinel-1 OPERA RTC-S1 (path 21, descending, VV+VH, 30 m) — 18 quarterly dates for the whole Dead Sea, 29 for Potash City, all one geometry so dates are comparable.
  • Converts power to dB, removes a scene-wide median offset, then produces four layers: false color, backscatter, change (date minus reference), and a water mask from an automatic (Otsu) threshold on VH, each water area carrying a ±1.5 dB detection band.
  • Everything ships as small static files (WebP/COG-style assets, JSON manifests) — no backend in the map itself, no build step, works from a local folder.

Findings (all verified against the data)

  • Dead Sea central water estimate fell from 812.3 km² (May 2016) to 702.2 km² (Oct 2026), −13.6%, with overlapping uncertainty bands stated.
  • 2017 estimates swung 690.6–834.5 km²; February was the lowest date of every year 2017–2020 (690.6–730.6 km²) — flagged as a hypothesis to test, not a result.
  • Potash City ponds: −8.8% central estimate; cause unattributed because radar cannot see brine chemistry.

Why it matters / impact

  • Water-resources and industrial monitoring teams get screening tools with uncertainty, not over-claims; students get a guided tour; the pattern is directly applicable to NISAR L-band as its record grows.

Creative + factors considered

  • The differentiators: Echo (LLM guide scoped to app facts, key held server-side, offline answers so a demo never fails), a one-per-year timeline instead of a 100-label axis, a color-blind-safe legend with text labels, honesty-first design (bands, hypothesis framing, "what we do not claim").
  • Considered: same-geometry rule, seasonal vs lasting change, wind roughening, salt crusts, short record and the May 2020–Oct 2026 gap, accessibility on phones.

Tools

  • Python 3.12 (rasterio/geospatial stack) for the pipeline; vanilla HTML/CSS/JS + Leaflet for the site (no framework, no build); Vercel serverless function + OpenAI API for Echo; GitHub for the code.
